content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper presents a MCTS method for performing search in spaces with continuous actions and states. The novelty is to use a directed acyclic graph (DAG) representing the searched space. The n-th layer of the DAG represents the states in the n-th decision in the environment. The statistics of the rollout policy are accumulated in the vertices of the DAG for which the states selected in search are associated with.  The states observed in search are clustered into different vertices of the DAG.

The approach is evaluated in several continuous control problems where one assumes that a perfect model is available. The baselines are CEM and MCTS with progressive widening. The results show that the proposed method often performs better than the baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths

The idea of representing sets of states as a DAG is interesting. This allows the search to separate the states encountered in search and possibly learn different tree policies for different vertices in the DAG. 

Another strength is the positive results on a somewhat large and diverse set of control problems. 

Weaknesses

Perhaps the main weakness of the paper is the lack of information about the proposed method. Many concepts are used without being defined and important information is left out of the paper. I apologize in advance if I missed the information I will list below and I kindly ask the author to correct me in their rebuttal. 

1. It isn't clear what is the object function for clustering nor the features used to cluster the states. Is this problem-dependent? What does it mean that two states are clustered together? Is it because they have similar utility value or because they are similar according to some domain-dependent function? 
2. The data structure used to store information about the search is a graph, but the paper treats it as a tree. For example, the sentence "... until a leaf nodes or a terminal node is reached." While I understand what a leaf node is in a tree, this isn't clear for graphs in general. Terminal nodes aren't defined either, but I can imagine this is when an episode finishes. I believe the method constructs a Direct Acyclic Graph (DAG) as the agent can only move in one direction (i.e., it cannot go back in time) so that no cycles are possible. If the solution was formalized as a DAG, then the term "leaf" would make more sense, but the correct term would be "sink nodes".
3. Many terms are used without being defined: layer, leaf, replay memory, function p in argmax function. 
4. The problem that the MCTS algorithm is set to solve wasn't defined formally. I understand that state and actions are continuous but time is discrete. These aren't defined in the paper, it is up to the reader to figure them out. 
5. The paper could provide more insights of why the method works and why it doesn't. What is the intuitive behind the DAG that makes the search algorithm more effective? 
6. The dispersion metric (the paper doesn't explain which metric is used, but let's say it is variance) shown in Figure 4 seems to be off to me. For example, in cartpole-balance_sparse the variance seems to be zero for the budget of 1.5k. Does that mean that for all 10 seeds the score was exactly 1.0? But for 0.5k was around 0.25 and for 2.5k was around 0.5? This seems like an odd result and I would double check whether the mean and variance are correct in Figure 4.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
As listed in the weaknesses above, the paper misses important definitions and doesn't provide a proper formalization of the approach. Some of the missing information affects reproducibility. For example, Table 1 doesn't specify the hyperparameters used in the Agglomerative clustering algorithm. I also do not known how to run the clustering algorithm because I do not know which features are used for clustering. 

The idea of creating a DAG and searching over it is interesting and novel, to the best of my knowledge.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The manuscript presents an interesting idea with reasonable empirical results, but the formalization and presentation are likely below the acceptance bar. The lack of a formal definition of the data structures used in the algorithm as well as of the problem the algorithm is set to solve muddies the water. I am unable to fully understand the method. 

Moreover, the dispersion metric and mean results in Figure 4 seem to be off. This is because the variance is somewhat large for a budget value and suddenly goes to zero and then increases again. I kindly ask the authors to verify the correctness of the plots and, if they are correct, I ask them to explain in the rebuttal how these results are possible.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper proposes a MCTS variant in continuous domain, where the graph structure is exploited by the algorithm.
The proposed algorithm is tested on several standard toy domains with competitive results against two baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The main idea of the paper is the clustering of (continuous) states in nodes and using the graph structure of tree. In discrete domains, similar situations arise with transpositions, and while there were a few attempts to deal with transpositions, none of the approaches is well established. Unfortunately, this paper is not discussing the theoretical implications either. In fact, even the algorithmic details of the action selection is discussed rather superficially, so the reader would have a hard time to understand the exact implementation of this step (along others). Therefore, it is difficult to evaluate the soundness of the algorithm.  

The illustrative example is interesting (although one needs a fair amount of guess-work to understand it). The experimental results show that CMCGS is competitive with CEM, although a conclusion of superiority would be far fetched.

It is unclear whether other elements, such as the clustering, should be regarded as novel elements, but there are no claims in this direction, and these are not discussed in detail either.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper leaves out too many details, and therefore understanding the relevance of the paper is difficult. The approach does not seem too novel, and the new ideas do not appear sufficiently sound theoretically.

The paper provides insufficient details to be able to reproduce the results, but the supplementary material might come at aid on this respect.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper is poorly written, with insufficient details, and discussion regarding the core contribution of the paper. The experiments show that the proposed algorithm is competitive, but it is hardly a convincing proof of superiority over the state-of-the-art.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposed Continuous Monte Carlo Graph Search (CMCGS), an extension of MCTS algorithm to online planning for solving decision making problems with continuous state and action spaces. CMCGS builds a layered search graph. In each layer, states are clustered into several stochastic action bandit nodes. Thus, CMCGS can solve complex continuous control problems with small search graphs. The authors claim that CMCGS outperforms CEM and MCTS-PW, especially when using small simulation budgets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
1. From the perspective of simulation budget, the proposed method CMCGS outperforms other methods when using small simulation budgets.
2. It is an interesting idea to apply graphs to Monte Carlo Tree Search.
 
Weaknesses
1. The experiments are not persuasive since the authors did not compare their method to current SOTA methods, such as Sampled MuZero (Hubert et al. (2021)). Although the author gave the explanation and put it to future work: “It has been shown that MCTS could benefit from learned value functions … We believe that this could be a trivial next step for improving the performance of CMCGS.” However, as the authors claim it is trivial, it will be more convincing if they demonstrate applying a learned value function to CMCGS and comparing it to SOTA methods directly.
2. The width expansion is applied to each layer in CMCGS backpropagation. This may lead to a high time complexity while running MCTS. The author should analyze the time complexity for calculating clustering and compare the methods by using time instead of simulation count.
3. Why do the authors decide to use Agglomerative clustering? There are many clustering methods. The authors should consider using different clustering methods in experiments. 
 
Other minor comments:
1. For Method 4.1(b), the author should clearly explain the definition of “low depth” and “enough experience”.
2. The c_t^* in Algorithm 2 line 32 is not defined or explained.
3. “Continous” in Conclusion should be “Continuous”.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
* Clarity: Well organized and written. Only some definition details are missing or unclear.
* Quality: The paper appears to be technically sound.
* Novelty: It is an interesting idea to apply graphs to Monte Carlo Tree Search.
* Reproducibility: The authors provide the source code in the supplementary material.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper proposed Continuous Monte Carlo Graph Search (CMCGS) by applying graphs to Monte Carlo Tree Search. The authors claim that CMCGS outperforms other methods like CEM and MCTS-PW, especially when using small simulation budgets. However, it will be more convincing if the authors provide more experimental results for comparing the proposed method to current SOTA methods.

content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.title: Withdrawal notice
content.comment: We would like to thank the reviewers for writing the insightful reviews of our paper and we very much appreciate the large time investment by both the reviewers and the area chair. We have created a clear plan how to improve the paper taking the feedback into account. However, in order to implement the plan properly, under time constraints, we have decided to withdraw the submission. We will do our best to address the reviews by adding further details and evaluations to the paper before submitting it to another venue.
